# bridge-jspace

**Question.** To answer a two-step question, a model first finds an entity in between (the **bridge**) and then uses it. A lens called **J++** reads hidden states as words. Does the model use the bridge in that word-like form, or does it reach it another way? And does that depend on what the model does with the bridge next?

> **Example.** "Iris picked the frog. The locker of the frog is 5. …" The bridge is *frog*.
> - **Lookup:** "Which locker belongs to Iris's pick?" The answer is written in the prompt.
> - **Recall:** "How many legs does Iris's pick have?" The answer comes from the model's memory.

**Status (24 Oct 2026).**
- Models: Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B. Qwen3.5-122B passed its hardware gate; its run is next.
- All numbers are unverified (not yet hand-checked); the layers, the rule and Dan's predictions were fixed before any result was opened. Built at 43d45ba8 from the X0 run files. Full log: [jobs/c3/X0.md](jobs/c3/X0.md).

## Main findings

1. **Recall needs the bridge's J++ form.** Removing the J++ part of a bridge change costs recalls 0.53 (9B) and 0.77 (27B) of their answer flips. A random part of the same size costs 0.04 and 0.03.
2. **It is specific to J++.** At the same size, the logit-lens directions, the input embeddings and random directions do nothing comparable.
3. **Lookups need the J++ form much less, and the two models differ.**
   - **9B:** the lookup does not need it, at any number of J++ atoms (extra loss −0.02 at 25 atoms to −0.17 at 200, on a rerun of the same scenes). The pre-registered test: **confirmed**.
   - **27B:** the lookup needs it a little at 25 atoms, so the pre-registered test was **not confirmed**. At 100 atoms (same rerun) it needs it about as much as recall does (0.60 vs 0.67).
4. **Not a missing digit.** Lookups flip mostly when the locker sentence comes *before* the pick sentence, so the lookup might read a locker number already attached to the bridge word, which our letter-only J++ dictionary cannot remove. It does not: with every token allowed, digits included, the 27B lookup's extra loss is 0.13 (letters only: 0.14), and the 10 digit directions alone give 0.00 on both models.

![Removing the J++ part costs recall far more than lookup](figures/status_2026-10-24/f1_readers.png)

## How we test it

- **Change the bridge.** Make a copy of the prompt where Iris picks a different animal (frog → tick). At one layer, take the difference between the two hidden states at the bridge word.
- **Paste the change back in three ways:**
  - whole;
  - without its J++ part (the 25 J++ directions that best describe it);
  - without a random part of the same size.
- **Ask both questions on the same patched prompt.** The question comes after the patch, so both readers get the exact same edit. Any difference comes from the reader, not the edit.
- **Measure** how many answers flip to the new animal's answer. The key number is the **extra loss**: the flips lost without the J++ part, minus the flips lost without the random part, both as shares of the whole change's flips.

## Results at the pre-registered layer

| Model, layer | Lookup: extra loss | Recall: extra loss | Rule | Recall minus lookup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 9B, 12 | −0.03 [−0.08, 0.03] | 0.50 [0.41, 0.57] | **confirmed** | 0.53 [0.42, 0.61] |
| 27B, 32 | 0.14 [0.08, 0.20] | 0.74 [0.66, 0.80] | **not confirmed** | 0.60 [0.50, 0.69] |

How to read this:
- The rule asked for a lookup extra loss of at most 0.10, and for recalls to lose at least 0.30 of their flips without the J++ part.
- In answer counts (27B, 200 scenes): lookups go 86 → 71 without J++ and 86 → 83 without the random part; recalls go 150 → 35 and 150 → 146.
- Scope: almost all of the lookup's flips at the bridge word come from scenes where the locker sentence comes before the pick; the lookup results describe those scenes.
- 95% intervals come from resampling the bridge entities (40 on the 9B, 44 on the 27B).

![Recall depends on the J++ form at every depth; lookup only early](figures/status_2026-10-24/f2_depth.png)

![On the 27B, with more J++ atoms the lookup needs J++ too](figures/status_2026-10-24/f5_atoms.png)

![It is J++, not any dictionary](figures/status_2026-10-24/f3_dictionaries.png)

![Adding the digit tokens to J++ changes nothing](figures/status_2026-10-24/f6_digits.png)

## What did not hold

- **"Past mid-depth, lookups don't use the J++ form at all."** It holds on the 9B. On the 27B it holds only when the change is pasted across the whole context (lookups 84% → 87% without J++, recalls 77% → 36%). That repeats a 23 Oct result on fresh scenes, but at the bridge word alone it does not hold.
- **"The lookup reads the answer digit at the bridge word"** (stated before the check). Digit tokens change nothing (above), and the J++ readout at the bridge word ranks the lookup's answer digit first in 13% of items (27B; chance is 10%).
- **Prompts without the chat template.** Can't test: the models open a thinking block or answer in markdown. This says nothing about the question.

## Weak spots we know about

| Weak spot | Status |
|---|---|
| The lookup's route at the bridge word is still unknown: not J++ on the 9B, not a digit on either model | X2' and X4 (9B) |
| Lookup flips depend on sentence order: locker before pick 76%–86%, after 9%–19% | figure F4; the next experiments fix the order |
| The edit changes two picks, not one: the 27B lookup's extra loss is 0.16 where the second change comes first, 0.08 where it does not (too few flips to measure) | a single-change version is next |
| On the 27B, the lookup's drop with depth follows how much of the change J++ captures (Spearman 0.79) | stated beside the depth figure |
| Two models from one family, generated scenes only | 122B next (gate passed); diverse and natural-text sets planned |
